opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, what I find really compelling about SleepFM is that it takes a data source we've been underusing for decades and shows how much signal was sitting there the whole time.

A polysomnography study is an incredibly rich recording. You have brain activity from EEG, heart activity from ECG, muscle activity, eye movements, breathing and airflow, and oxygen saturation, all captured continuously for an entire night. Clinically, though, most of that gets compressed into a handful of summary numbers, like an apnea-hypopnea index or sleep staging. That's useful, but it throws away almost everything about how those systems interact over eight hours.

What SleepFM does is treat the whole thing as one multimodal signal and learn representations across those channels together. I think that's the key insight. A lot of disease isn't visible in any one channel. It shows up in the coupling: how your heart rhythm responds to a breathing disruption, or how cortical activity and autonomic activity move together across sleep stages. A model that learns jointly across modalities can pick up on those cross-system patterns in a way a single-channel model or a human scoring a chart probably can't.

The other thing I find interesting is the foundation model framing itself. Rather than building one narrow model per condition, you pretrain on a large amount of unlabeled sleep data and then find that the same representation predicts a pretty broad range of future conditions, including cardiovascular, metabolic, neurological, and even mortality risk. That generality suggests sleep is acting as a kind of stress test for the whole body. You're observing physiology in a relatively controlled state for hours, which is something you basically never get in a normal clinic visit.

There's also a nice lesson for medical AI more broadly. We often assume progress depends on getting more labeled data, but some of the biggest wins come from finding modalities that are already dense and already collected at scale, and letting self-supervised learning extract structure from them.

That said, I'd want to see a lot more before this changes care. Sleep studies aren't done on a random slice of the population. People are usually referred because something is already wrong, so you have to think carefully about selection effects and how well results generalize across sites, equipment, and demographics. And prediction isn't the same as actionability. Knowing someone has elevated risk is only valuable if there's a sensible intervention and a workflow that gets it to the right clinician.

But directionally, I think it's a really exciting example of where this field is going: multimodal, physiology-rich signals, general-purpose representations, and eventually maybe moving some of this out of the sleep lab and into wearables, where you could get this kind of signal far more often and for far more people.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So what I find really compelling about SleepFM is that it takes seriously how rich a sleep study actually is. A polysomnogram isn't one signal, it's a whole bundle: EEG for brain activity, EOG for eye movements, EMG for muscle tone, ECG for the heart, respiratory channels, oxygen saturation. Historically, each of those has been read by a specialist for one narrow purpose, like staging sleep or scoring apneas. Most of the information in that night of data just gets thrown away.

The interesting move is to treat all of those modalities as different views of the same underlying physiological state, and to learn a joint representation across them in a self-supervised way, without needing labels for every disease up front. You're essentially asking the model to figure out how the brain, heart, and breathing signals relate to each other over the course of a night, and that cross-modal structure turns out to be where a lot of the health signal lives. Something subtle in the coupling between heart rate variability and respiration, or between arousals and oxygen dips, might not be visible in any single channel on its own.

And then the payoff is that once you have that representation, you can ask it about things sleep medicine wasn't designed to ask. Can we predict future cardiovascular risk, or neurodegenerative conditions, or metabolic disease, from a single night? The early results suggest yes, and in some cases the sleep-derived predictions are competitive with or complementary to standard clinical risk factors.

What I think is genuinely important here is the framing: sleep as a window into the body, not just a thing to be diagnosed in itself. We spend a third of our lives in a state where the body is running a fairly stereotyped program, which makes it a very clean setting for detecting deviations. If foundation models can make that window readable, you start to imagine a future where a night of sleep data becomes a routine health signal, not a rare specialist test. There are real questions about generalization across populations, about what happens when you move from lab polysomnography to wearables, and about how clinicians act on a probabilistic risk score. But as a demonstration of what multimodal physiological foundation models can do, I think it's one of the more exciting examples we have.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is the idea that sleep is a window into your broader health. A sleep study captures several systems at once—brain activity, breathing, heart activity—and the relationships between those signals may tell you something that none of them tells you on its own.

So the promise of a multimodal model is that it can learn patterns across those systems, rather than treating each measurement as a separate diagnostic test. You can imagine disrupted breathing and changes in heart activity meaning something different depending on what’s happening in the brain at that moment.

The question I’d want to probe is how well those predictions generalize. Does the model work across hospitals and patient populations? Is it picking up early signs of disease, or evidence of a condition that’s already present? And does knowing the prediction actually let you intervene in a useful way? That’s the exciting possibility: turning a sleep study into a broader opportunity for early detection.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that sleep is a window into a lot of different physiological systems at once. You have brain activity, heart activity, breathing, oxygen levels—and the relationships between those signals can be more informative than any one signal on its own.

So the exciting idea with SleepFM is to learn a shared representation of all of that, rather than building a separate model around a handful of features for each disease. That representation could capture patterns that are useful across many different prediction tasks.

The distinction I’d want to keep clear, though, is between predicting a future diagnosis and understanding what’s causing it. A model might be detecting early signs of disease, or risk factors, or something about who gets a sleep study. The compelling next step is to establish how well those predictions generalize and whether they actually help clinicians make better decisions.
